questions.stem: A point moves so that x(t) = 2 + 3t and y(t) = 1 − 4t. What is its speed?
questions.explanation: The velocity is [x′(t), y′(t)] = [3, −4], so the speed is √(3² + (−4)²) = 5. Adding the components gives 7, which is not the magnitude of a vector.

questions.stem: A point moves so that x(t) = 2 + 3t and y(t) = 1 − 4t. What is the Cartesian equation of its path?
questions.explanation: From x = 2 + 3t, t = (x − 2)/3, so y = 1 − 4(x − 2)/3, giving 3y = 11 − 4x, or 4x + 3y = 11. Check: t = 1 gives (5, −3) and 20 − 9 = 11.

questions.stem: A point starts at (1, 2) and moves with constant velocity [2, 5]. Where is it at t = 3?
questions.explanation: Uniform motion gives (x(t), y(t)) = (1 + 2t, 2 + 5t), so at t = 3 the point is (7, 17). The value (6, 15) is the displacement 3[2, 5] without the starting position.

questions.stem: Particle A has position (1 + 2t, 3 + t) and particle B has position (10 − t, −3 + 3t), for t ≥ 0. Do they collide?
options: No, their paths cross but at different times
Yes, at t = 2, at the point (5, 5)
No, their paths are parallel and never meet
Yes, at t = 3, at the point (7, 6)
questions.explanation: Setting 1 + 2t = 10 − t gives t = 3, and then both y-coordinates are 6, so both particles are at (7, 6) at the same time. At t = 2, A is at (5, 5) but B is at (8, 3).

questions.stem: Particle A has position (t, 2t) and particle B has position (4 − t, t), for t ≥ 0. Which statement is true?
options: Their paths are parallel lines, so they never meet
Their paths cross at (4/3, 8/3), but they reach it at different times
questions.explanation: The paths are y = 2x and y = 4 − x, which cross at (4/3, 8/3). A is there when t = 4/3, but B is there when t = 8/3, so they do not collide. At t = 2, B is at (2, 2), not (2, 4).

questions.stem: A ball is hit from ground level on flat ground and its position after t seconds is x = 15t, y = 20t − 4.9t², in metres. What is its initial speed?
questions.explanation: The initial velocity is [x′(0), y′(0)] = [15, 20], whose magnitude is √(15² + 20²) = 25 m s⁻¹. Adding the components gives 35, and 20 is only the vertical component.

questions.stem: A ball is hit from ground level on flat ground and its position after t seconds is x = 15t, y = 20t − 4.9t², in metres. When does it land?
questions.explanation: It lands when y = 0: t(20 − 4.9t) = 0, so t = 20/4.9 ≈ 4.08 s. The value 2.04 s is when it reaches its highest point, halfway through the flight.

questions.stem: A ball is hit from ground level on flat ground and its position after t seconds is x = 15t, y = 20t − 4.9t², in metres. What is its greatest height?
questions.explanation: The height is greatest when y′(t) = 20 − 9.8t = 0, at t ≈ 2.04 s, giving y = 20 × 2.04 − 4.9 × 2.04² ≈ 20.4 m. The value 61.2 m is the horizontal range.

questions.stem: A ball is hit from ground level on flat ground and its position after t seconds is x = 15t, y = 20t − 4.9t², in metres. What is its speed at t = 1?
questions.explanation: The velocity is [15, 20 − 9.8t], which is [15, 10.2] at t = 1, so the speed is √(15² + 10.2²) ≈ 18.1 m s⁻¹. Adding the components gives 25.2, and 25.0 is the launch speed.

questions.stem: A ball is hit from ground level on flat ground and its position after t seconds is x = 15t, y = 20t − 4.9t², in metres. What is the Cartesian equation of its path?
questions.explanation: Substituting t = x/15 gives y = 20(x/15) − 4.9(x/15)² = (4/3)x − 4.9x²/225, a parabola. Dividing x² by 15 instead of 15² gives the third form.

questions.stem: A ball is thrown from the point (0, 2) with initial velocity [8, 6] m s⁻¹, so x = 8t and y = 2 + 6t − 4.9t². How high is it when it has travelled 4 m horizontally?
questions.explanation: x = 4 when t = 0.5, so y = 2 + 3 − 4.9 × 0.25 ≈ 3.78 m. Leaving out the starting height gives 1.78 m, and ignoring gravity gives 5.00 m.

questions.stem: A point moves so that x = t² and y = 2t, for all real t. What is the Cartesian equation of its path?
questions.explanation: From y = 2t, t = y/2, so x = (y/2)² = y²/4, giving y² = 4x. This is a parabola opening to the right; swapping the roles of x and y gives x² = 4y.

questions.stem: A point moves so that x = t + 1 and y = t² − 3. What is the Cartesian equation of its path?
questions.explanation: t = x − 1, so y = (x − 1)² − 3 = x² − 2x + 1 − 3 = x² − 2x − 2. Using t = x + 1 by mistake gives x² + 2x − 2.

questions.stem: A point moves so that x = eᵗ and y = e²ᵗ, for all real t. Which describes its path?
options: The part of the line y = 2x for which x > 0
The part of y = x² for which x < 0
The part of y = x² for which x > 0
questions.explanation: y = (eᵗ)² = x², but x = eᵗ is always positive, so only the right half of the parabola is traced. Eliminating t without checking the possible values of x wrongly gives the whole parabola.

questions.stem: A point moves so that x = 4cos(t) and y = 3sin(t). What is the Cartesian equation of its path?
questions.explanation: cos(t) = x/4 and sin(t) = y/3, and cos²(t) + sin²(t) = 1 gives x²/16 + y²/9 = 1, an ellipse. Forgetting to square the 4 and the 3 gives the second form.

questions.stem: A point moves along a curve. How is its velocity vector [x′(t), y′(t)] related to the curve?
options: It points towards the centre of the curve's bend
It is tangent to the curve at the point's position
It is perpendicular to the curve at the point's position
It points from the origin to the point's position
questions.explanation: By the chain rule, dy/dx = y′(t)/x′(t), which is the gradient of the curve, so the velocity vector always lies along the tangent. The vector from the origin is the position vector, not the velocity.

questions.stem: A point has position (t², t³). What is its velocity vector?
questions.explanation: The velocity is the vector of derivatives, [x′(t), y′(t)] = [2t, 3t²]. The vector [2, 6t] is the second derivative, which is the acceleration.

questions.stem: A point has position (t³ − t, t² + 1). What is its velocity at t = 1?
questions.explanation: x′(t) = 3t² − 1 and y′(t) = 2t, so at t = 1 the velocity is [2, 2]. The pair [0, 2] is the position at t = 1, not the velocity.

questions.stem: A curve is given by x = 2t + 1 and y = t³ − 3t. What is the gradient dy/dx at t = 2?
questions.explanation: dy/dx = y′(t)/x′(t) = (3t² − 3)/2, which is 9/2 at t = 2. Dividing the other way gives 2/9.

questions.stem: A curve is given by x = t² and y = t³. What is the equation of its tangent at t = 1?
questions.explanation: At t = 1 the point is (1, 1) and dy/dx = 3t²/(2t) = 3/2, so y − 1 = (3/2)(x − 1), giving y = (3x − 1)/2. Using y′(t) = 3 alone as the gradient gives y = 3x − 2.

questions.stem: A curve is given by x = t² − 2t and y = t³. At which point is its tangent vertical?
questions.explanation: The tangent is vertical where x′(t) = 0 and y′(t) ≠ 0. x′(t) = 2t − 2 = 0 at t = 1, where y′ = 3 ≠ 0, giving the point (−1, 1). At (0, 0), where t = 0, y′ = 0 and the tangent is horizontal.

questions.stem: A particle has position (t² − 4t, t³ − 12t) for t ≥ 0. When and where is it momentarily at rest?
options: It is never at rest for t ≥ 0
questions.explanation: At rest means the velocity [2t − 4, 3t² − 12] is the zero vector, and both components are zero at t = 2. The position then is (4 − 8, 8 − 24) = (−4, −16).

questions.stem: How is the speed of a point moving with position (x(t), y(t)) found?
questions.explanation: Speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector [x′(t), y′(t)]. The expression √(x(t)² + y(t)²) is the distance from the origin, and y′(t)/x′(t) is the gradient dy/dx.

questions.stem: A point has position (t², 2t). What is its speed at t = 2?
questions.explanation: The velocity is [2t, 2] = [4, 2] at t = 2, so the speed is √(16 + 4) = √20 = 2√5. The value 4√2 is the distance of the position (4, 4) from the origin.

questions.stem: A point has position (2t, t² − 4t). What is its least speed, and when does it occur?
questions.explanation: The velocity is [2, 2t − 4], so the speed is √(4 + (2t − 4)²), least when 2t − 4 = 0, at t = 2, where it is 2. The speed is never 0 because the x-component is always 2.

questions.stem: A point in 3D has position (t, t², t³). What is its speed at t = 1?
questions.explanation: The velocity is [1, 2t, 3t²] = [1, 2, 3] at t = 1, so the speed is √(1 + 4 + 9) = √14. The value √3 is the distance of the position (1, 1, 1) from the origin.

questions.stem: A point moves along a curve from t = a to t = b. Which integral gives the length of the path?
options: ∫ from a to b of √(x′(t)² + y′(t)²) dt
∫ from a to b of (x′(t) + y′(t)) dt
∫ from a to b of √(x(t)² + y(t)²) dt
∫ from a to b of (x′(t)² + y′(t)²) dt
questions.explanation: The arc length is the integral of the speed, √(v · v), over the time interval. Leaving out the square root integrates the square of the speed, which is not a length.

questions.stem: A point moves with x = 1 + 3t and y = 2 + 4t. How far does it travel from t = 0 to t = 2?
questions.explanation: The speed is constant at √(3² + 4²) = 5, so the length of the path is the integral of 5 from 0 to 2, which is 10. The value 14 comes from adding the components instead of finding the magnitude.

questions.stem: What is the length of the curve x = 3t², y = 2t³ from t = 0 to t = 1?
questions.explanation: The speed is √(36t² + 36t⁴) = 6t√(1 + t²). Its antiderivative is 2(1 + t²)^(3/2), so the length is 2(2√2) − 2(1) = 4√2 − 2. Forgetting to subtract the value at t = 0 gives 4√2.

questions.stem: A curve has x = t²/2 and y = (1/3)(2t + 1)^(3/2). What is its length from t = 0 to t = 2?
questions.explanation: x′(t) = t and y′(t) = (2t + 1)^(1/2), so the speed is √(t² + 2t + 1) = t + 1. The integral of t + 1 from 0 to 2 is 2 + 2 = 4.

questions.stem: A point moves around a circle of radius R with position [R cos(t), R sin(t)]. Which calculation confirms the circumference of the circle?
options: ∫ from 0 to π of R dt = πR
questions.explanation: The velocity is [−R sin(t), R cos(t)], whose magnitude is √(R²(sin²(t) + cos²(t))) = R. One full revolution takes t from 0 to 2π, so the length is 2πR. Integrating from 0 to π covers only half the circle.

questions.stem: A point in 3D moves along the helix (4cos(t), 4sin(t), 3t). How far does it travel from t = 0 to t = 2π?
questions.explanation: The velocity is [−4sin(t), 4cos(t), 3], whose magnitude is √(16 + 9) = 5 at all times, so the length is 5 × 2π = 10π. The value 8π is the circumference of the circle the helix winds around, ignoring the climb.

questions.stem: A point has position P(t) = [cos(t), sin(t)] for t ≥ 0. Which describes its motion?
options: Around the unit circle anticlockwise from (1, 0), at speed 1
Around the unit circle clockwise from (1, 0), at speed 1
Around the unit circle anticlockwise from (0, 1), at speed 2π
Along the line y = x from the origin, at speed 1
questions.explanation: At t = 0 the point is at (1, 0), and as t increases the angle increases, so it moves anticlockwise. The velocity [−sin(t), cos(t)] has magnitude 1, so the speed is constant at 1.

questions.stem: A point moves with position [3cos(2t), 3sin(2t)]. What is its speed?
questions.explanation: The velocity is [−6sin(2t), 6cos(2t)], with magnitude 6. In general, [R cos(ωt), R sin(ωt)] has speed Rω. The value 12 is the size of the acceleration, Rω².

questions.stem: A point moves with position P(t) = [R cos(ωt), R sin(ωt)]. What is its acceleration?
options: −ωP(t), directed towards the centre with magnitude Rω
Zero, because the point moves at a constant speed
−ω²P(t), directed towards the centre with magnitude Rω²
ω²P(t), directed away from the centre with magnitude Rω²
questions.explanation: Differentiating twice gives [−Rω² cos(ωt), −Rω² sin(ωt)] = −ω²P(t), which points back towards the centre: centripetal acceleration of size Rω². The speed is constant, but the direction of the velocity keeps changing, so the acceleration is not zero.

questions.stem: A point moves with position [3cos(2t), 3sin(2t)]. How long does it take to go once around its circle?
questions.explanation: One revolution needs the angle 2t to increase by 2π, so t increases by π. The value 2π would be the period for [3cos(t), 3sin(t)].

questions.stem: A particle has position (3cos(t), 2sin(2t)). What is its speed at t = π/2?
questions.explanation: The velocity is [−3sin(t), 4cos(2t)], which at t = π/2 is [−3, 4cos(π)] = [−3, −4], with magnitude 5. Adding the sizes of the components gives 7.

questions.stem: A point moves with position [2sin(t), 2cos(t)] for t ≥ 0. Where does it start, and which way does it go around the circle?
questions.explanation: At t = 0 the position is (2sin(0), 2cos(0)) = (0, 2). The velocity there is [2cos(0), −2sin(0)] = [2, 0], pointing right from the top of the circle, so the motion is clockwise.
